newsitem.title: USA: IBM CEO sees many growth opportunities.
newsitem.headline: IBM CEO sees many growth opportunities.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp Chairman and CEO Louis Gerstner said that there are many opportunities for growth within IBM, but he also reiterated IBM's financial goal of high single-digit revenue growth.

"We have enormous opportunities within IBM," Gerstner said in his fourth annual meeting with Wall Street analysts. But because of IBM's size, the $76 billion giant will not grow at the explosive rates of some "meteor"-like technology firms.
"Our model is to procure high single-digit revenue growth," Gerstner told analysts.
"We are not going to be like most information technology companies," Gerstner said. "We are not going to grow 40 to 50 percent a year. That's hard to do."

In its most recent first quarter earnings report, IBM had revenue growth of nine percent, on a constant currency basis. The company had stellar growth in its services business, which grew 28 percent, amid a drop in some hardware revenues, such as mainframes, minicomputers and workstations.
Analysts asked Gerstner if he ever expects to see IBM's System 390 mainframes, once the company's biggest revenue and profit generator, growing again.

Gerstner said that in the past three years, IBM has slashed prices of mainframes by 80 percent, which has helped fuel stronger demand. And with more and more computers linked on corporate networks accessing the massive amounts of data stored in these machines, demand for these big data repositories grows. But Gerstner declined to predict growth.

"I'm not going to count on the 390 becoming a great growth engine again, as much as Linda (Sanford, general manager of IBM's System 390 business) will tell me just watch," Gerstner said, adding that he has also lived through too many price wars as a former customer, before he joined IBM in April 1993.

Instead, Gerstner pointed to software and services as its growth engines, but he added that software has not yet performed as well as its services business because the company clung to its software that run on its host mainframe systems, instead of developing distributed software.

"We are the Rodney Dangerfield of the software industry," Gerstner joked, referring to the comedian whose mantra was he did not get any respect. "And to a certain extent, we deserve it. We gave software away on our hardware, we watched software go distributed and we hung onto our host stuff."
Total software sales fell 2.9 percent in the first quarter.
The decline was mostly attributable to mainframe software.
But Gerstner said that a new growth area for IBM is in distributed and so-called "middleware" software, which connects its host mainframe software to other diverse computers.

IBM's purchases of Tivoli Systems and of Lotus Development Corp were strategic investments in this area, Gerstner said. "We are feeling pretty good and we think it can be a growth business," he said of IBM's distributed software.
He also told analysts that IBM's hard disk drive business had such high double-digit growth that it was almost at three digits. And personal computers have made a huge comeback.
"Four years ago Compaq was kicking sand in our face," Gerstner said. In the first quarter, IBM's PC unit growth and PC revenue growth outpaced Compaq's, the PC industry leader.

Gerstner also highlighted some of the "solutions" IBM has developed in the networked computing world, such as developing an application for American Airlines so that its customers could make reservations and buy tickets over the Internet.

"We have fixed the problems, we have created the growth opportunities," Gerstner said, adding that IBM executives do not sit around wondering how the company will grow. "It's not a question of will we execute, it's how well will we execute."
